summary:
Caribbean Netherlands consists of Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba, three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The islands stand under the Netherlands' national framework, and the anti-discrimination law applying there covers citizens and visitors alike, according to travel-facing coverage published by GayCities on 14 December 2022 and updated 1 September 2023.

That coverage ranks Bonaire fifth among destinations in the Caribbean and Latin America that celebrate marriage equality, on the stated basis that the island's position as part of the Netherlands places its citizens and visitors under strict anti-discrimination laws and that same-sex couples are warmly welcomed.

Marriage between two people of the same sex has been registrable in the islands since 2012. The first such marriage was recorded by the Census Office in Saba on 4 December 2012, between Aruban Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, 26, and Venezuelan Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, 27, both visiting residents.

Civil ceremonies on Saba run routinely through the island registry. Saba Tourism's official weddings page identifies the Court Room in the Administrative Building as the simplest venue for an efficient civil ceremony, and documents the registrar, Julieta Woods, as flexible with couples' wishes.
tangentialFactors:
The GayCities ranking is a travel publication's assessment rather than a legal source. It places Bonaire fifth in a regional list of destinations that celebrate marriage equality, a comparison across Caribbean and Latin American jurisdictions rather than a statement of Dutch law.

The first marriage registered in the islands joined two visiting residents, one from Aruba and one from Venezuela, so the registry's practice has from the outset served couples arriving from elsewhere rather than only local residents.
localsOnly:
Anti-discrimination protection in the islands covers citizens as well as visitors, so residents of Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba fall under the same statutory coverage described for travellers.

The civil registry practice documented on Saba dates to 2012 and operates through the island's own administrative offices, with the registrar's stated flexibility applying to local couples as well as visiting ones.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source sets out the text of the applicable anti-discrimination provisions, the penalties they carry, or any enforcement record, so the strength of protection behind the ranking cannot be verified.

Nothing in the sources covers identity-document or gender-marker rules for trans visitors, screening or border procedure, access to facilities, or hate-crime enforcement in the islands, and no trans-specific violence or official hostility is recorded there.

The ranking does not describe its methodology or the criteria behind Bonaire's fifth place.
